long_F.input: Today's Monday, December 1. Help me lay out this week: training, a final toast rehearsal, and staying sane at work.
long_F.reply:
Here’s a race-week plan for **Monday 1 December to Sunday 7 December**. It assumes your knee is currently pain-free. If it’s still cranky, replace runs with cycling/swimming and speak to your physio.

| Day | Training | Toast rehearsal | Work sanity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mon 1 Dec** | Rest, physio, mobility | Text/ask Mum about the photo if you haven’t already | Write 3 must-do tasks; block lunch; no new projects |
| **Tue 2 Dec** | Easy **5 km** before 7am, flat and conversational | Read opening + bike story aloud once | Do hardest task first; decline non-essential meetings |
| **Wed 3 Dec** | No run. 20–30 min cross-train or mobility | **Full 3-minute rehearsal aloud.** Record it, listen once, note where you rush | Keep meetings light; prep any handover |
| **Thu 4 Dec** | Easy **4–5 km** before 7am. Last run before race | Practise opening and closing only | Finish key items; don’t add new ones |
| **Fri 5 Dec** | No run. Walk, stretch, physio | Visualise the room and your first line | Tie up loose ends; set an out-of-office if possible |
| **Sat 6 Dec** | No run. Short walk. Prepare race kit: bib, shoes, clothes, breakfast, travel | No full rehearsal | Stay off email if you can |
| **Sun 7 Dec** | **Riverside Half** | No toast work | Rest after the race |

### Race-week nutrition  
From **Thursday to Saturday**, keep meals familiar and carb-focused, without suddenly adding lots of fibre. Drink enough that urine stays pale yellow, but don’t force huge amounts.

### Knee rule  
No back-to-back runs this week. If the knee feels sore after Tuesday, **skip Thursday’s run** and cross-train instead. On Sunday, run within yourself—don’t chase a time.

long_F.reply:
Here’s a clear structure for a 30-minute raise conversation with Daniel.

## Before the meeting

- Email Daniel to schedule 30 minutes and say: **“I’d like to discuss my role, responsibilities, and compensation.”** This avoids surprising him.
- Prepare a one-page summary with your achievements and the numbers below.
- Know your target figure or percentage, based on market data if possible.

---

## Conversation structure

### 1. Opening — 2 minutes

Thank him for the time, state the purpose simply:

> “Thanks for making time. I want to talk about the scope of my role and my compensation. I’ve taken on significantly more responsibility this year and delivered clear results, so I’d like to discuss a salary adjustment.”

### 2. Impact summary — 5–7 minutes

Lead with outcomes, not effort. Use 4–5 achievements with numbers:

- Led the **vendor portal project** from scoping to beta, working across teams and suppliers.
- Cut new supplier onboarding time from **three weeks to one**.
- Automated the monthly vendor report, saving about **six hours per month**—roughly 72 hours a year.
- Mentored **two junior analysts** through their first quarter.
- Presented Q2 results to the leadership team and ran the **data quality working group**.

Frame each as:

> “This saved time / reduced risk / improved X, and I’ve been doing it alongside my core role.”

Keep it tight and confident. Don’t apologise or say “sorry to ask.”

### 3. The ask — 2–3 minutes

Be specific:

> “Given the increased scope and these results, I’m asking for a raise to **[£X / X%]**. I believe that reflects the level I’m now working at and the market for this kind of work.”

If you have market data or examples of similar roles, mention it briefly, but don’t overwhelm.

### 4. Listen and discuss — 5–10 minutes

Pause and let Daniel respond. Don’t fill the silence.

Useful questions:

- “What are your thoughts?”
- “Is that something you’re able to consider?”
- “What would the process and timeline look like?”

### 5. Close with next steps — 2 minutes

If it’s positive:

> “That’s great—can we confirm the timeline and what you need from me?”

If he needs to think:

> “Thanks for considering it. When could we come back to this?”

If it’s a no or not now:

> “I understand. What specifically would make a salary increase possible, and can we review again in [1–3 months]?”

---

## Be ready for possible objections

- **“We don’t have budget right now.”**  
  Ask if a title/level review, one-off bonus, extra leave, or a formal review date is possible.

- **“The vendor portal slipped.”**  
  Acknowledge it briefly, focus on what you delivered and the risk you managed, without being defensive.

- **“You’re already at the top of the band.”**  
  Ask if the band can be reviewed, or if there’s a higher level role you’re already operating at.

---

## After the meeting

Send a short email:

> “Thanks for the conversation today. As discussed, my target is [£X / X%], and you said you’d come back by [date]. Happy to provide any further information.”

That creates a paper trail and keeps it moving. Good luck—you’ve got strong, measurable achievements to back this up.

long_F.input: What if my manager says the budget is frozen?
long_F.reply:
If Daniel says the budget is frozen, don’t treat that as the end of the conversation. Ask what the freeze actually means and shift the negotiation to **timing, alternatives, or a formal review**.

### Possible responses

**1. Ask when it will be reviewed**
> “I understand. When will the budget be reviewed, and could we agree a salary adjustment now to take effect then?”

This is useful because many freezes are temporary, but managers won’t volunteer a future date unless you ask.

**2. Ask about an exception**
> “Is there any exception process, or is this a company-wide freeze?”

Sometimes there’s headroom for retention or high performers even when general budgets are frozen.

**3. Ask what would make it possible**
> “What specifically would need to change for this to be approved—performance, scope, or budget timing?”

This turns a vague “no” into clear criteria you can meet.

**4. Propose a formal review date**
> “Could we schedule a formal review in three months with agreed objectives? If I meet them, I’d like the raise to be approved then.”

Try to get that in writing.

### If the freeze is genuine, negotiate non-salary items

Ask for things that may not hit the same budget line:

- A one-off bonus or retention payment
- Extra annual leave
- A title change or seniority uplift
- Flexible or reduced working hours
- Training budget or conference attendance
- Public recognition or a formal note in your file

For example:
> “If salary isn’t possible right now, is there flexibility on a one-off bonus, extra leave, or a title review?”

### Follow up by email

After the meeting, send something like:

> “Thanks for the conversation today. I understand the salary budget is currently frozen. As discussed, we’ll review again in [month] against [specific goals], and I’d appreciate it if the adjustment could take effect from that date. In the meantime, we also discussed [extra leave / title review / bonus].”

That creates a record and makes it harder for the issue to disappear.

### One caution

“Budget is frozen” can be a deflection. Your strongest move is to ask **when and under what conditions** it changes, rather than just accepting it. If the answer stays vague, that tells you something about how the company values retention.

long_F.input: I have one free Saturday to sort out the flat after the move: unpacked boxes, a broken shelf, and paperwork. Help me plan the day so it actually gets done.
long_F.reply:
Here’s a one-Saturday reset plan. The goal isn’t a perfect flat—it’s to leave the day feeling noticeably clearer.

## Evening before

- Gather tools: screwdriver/drill, screws, wood glue, tape measure, bin bags, marker, label stickers.
- Put a folder or tray in one place for “action paperwork”.
- Charge phone or speaker for music/podcast.
- Pick one room that will become the **priority room** tomorrow—usually kitchen, bedroom, or living room.

## Saturday plan

| Time | Task |
|---|---|
| 8:30–9:00 | Breakfast, open curtains/windows, put on music. Set up three zones: **Keep**, **Donate/return**, **Rubbish/recycling**. |
| 9:00–10:30 | **Paperwork blitz.** Sort everything into piles first: bills/finance, tenancy/move, work/benefits, manuals/warranties, shred. Don’t act on each item yet. Put anything urgent in the action folder. Use 25-minute timers. |
| 10:30–10:45 | Break. Step outside or make tea. |
| 10:45–12:00 | **Broken shelf.** Decide: fix now or replace later. Tighten brackets, re-drill wall anchors, or glue if simple. If it needs parts, photograph it, measure the space, and add it to a “replace” list—then move on. Don’t let this eat the day. |
| 12:00–12:30 | Lunch. Leave the flat if possible, even briefly. |
| 12:30–14:30 | **Unpacking blitz, round 1.** Work in one room or zone, not everywhere. Open one box fully before starting another. Put each item in the room where it belongs, don’t arrange perfectly yet. Flatten boxes immediately. |
| 14:30–14:45 | Break. |
| 14:45–16:15 | **Unpacking blitz, round 2.** Continue in the priority room. If you finish, start the next most-used space. Keep a “donate/return” box handy. |
| 16:15–17:00 | **Reset cleanup.** Break down boxes, take out rubbish/recycling, wipe surfaces, vacuum the main area. If the shelf is fixed, put it back in place. |
| 17:00–17:15 | **Close out.** Write down anything unfinished and schedule one short weekday session for it. Take a photo—it’ll help you see the progress. |

## Rules to make it work

- Don’t buy storage or décor on the day.
- Don’t deep-organise drawers while unpacking; just get things into rooms.
- Use the “only touch once” rule: as soon as you pick something up, decide keep/donate/return/rubbish.
- If the broken shelf needs a second trip or special parts, set a 10-minute limit to order or add it to a list.
- Paperwork doesn’t need to be fully resolved—just sorted into clear piles and one urgent file.

This should leave the flat calmer and give you a realistic finish line rather than an endless day.

- Paperwork only needs sorting, not acting on.
- The nap is part of the plan, not a reward for finishing everything.

If you only do paperwork and unpack one room, that’s still a successful day.

Hi Priya—great that you’re planning this early and listening to your physio. With the no-back-to-back-run-days rule, I’d keep the next month simple and conservative: **3 runs per week**, focused on consistency and knee tolerance.

### Weekly template

| Day | Plan |
|---|---|
| Monday | Rest / physio exercises / mobility |
| Tuesday | Easy run **before 7am** |
| Wednesday | Cross-train or strength after work |
| Thursday | Easy run **before 7am** |
| Friday | Rest / mobility |
| Saturday | Long run |
| Sunday | Walk, cycle, swim, or full rest |

This gives you at least one non-run day between every run day.

### Next-month run progression

| Week | Tuesday | Thursday | Saturday long run |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 1 | 5 km easy | 5 km easy | 8 km easy |
| Week 2 | 5 km easy | 6 km easy | 9 km easy |
| Week 3 | 6 km easy | 6 km easy | 10 km easy |
| Week 4 | 5 km easy | 5 km easy | 8–9 km easy stepback |

If weekday time is tight, do **30–40 minutes** instead of worrying about exact distance.

- Keep all runs at a **conversational pace**.
- If your knee feels off, swap that run for cycling/swimming and check with your physio.
- Add **2 strength sessions per week** focused on glutes, quads, calves, and single-leg stability.
- Increase total weekly distance slowly—your long run should only grow by about **1 km per week**.

long_N.input: Different project: my sister Anika is getting married on December 14 to Tomás, and I'm her maid of honour. I have to give a toast, three minutes max, and I genuinely dread public speaking. The story I want to use: when we were kids Anika taught me to ride a bike by pretending she was still holding the seat - she'd let go ages before and I only found out when I turned around. Can you help me with a structure?
long_N.reply:
The bike story is perfect for a toast: it’s short, visual, warm, and has a built-in meaning. Here’s a structure that keeps you under three minutes.

## Toast Structure: “The Bike Story”

### 1. Opening — about 15–20 seconds
Just say who you are and why you’re there.

> “Good evening everyone. For anyone who doesn’t know me, I’m [Name], Anika’s sister and very proud maid of honour.”

Optional: thank the guests/families briefly, then move on.

---

### 2. The bike story — about 40 seconds
Tell it simply. Don’t overexplain.

> “When we were kids, Anika taught me to ride a bike. She ran along behind me holding the seat, and I kept yelling, ‘Don’t let go!’ She kept promising she wouldn’t. She lied — kindly. By the time I finally turned around, she was way down the street, cheering.”

Pause after that line. Let people laugh or smile.

---

### 3. What it says about Anika — about 40 seconds
This is the “why this matters” moment.

> “That’s Anika. She has always known how to make someone feel supported until they realise they can do it themselves. She never needed the credit. She just wanted me to ride.”

Keep this to one or two sentences. Don’t turn it into a speech about childhood.

---

### 4. Connect it to Tomás and marriage — about 50 seconds
This is where the story becomes a wedding toast.

> “Tomás, watching you two together, I see that same steady, joyful trust. A good marriage is a bit like that bike ride: you hold each other up, you cheer from behind, and sometimes you trust enough to let go. Tomás, you’re now the person Anika turns around to see cheering.”

If you have a specific small observation about Tomás or them as a couple, add it here — one line is enough.

---

### 5. Close and toast — about 15–20 seconds
Make it clear you’re done.

> “So please raise your glasses. To Anika and Tomás — may you always keep each other steady, and may you always look back and realise how far you’ve come. To the bride and groom!”

Everyone drinks. Then you can sit down.

---

## Delivery tips for public speaking nerves

- **Write only bullet points on a card**, not full paragraphs.
- **Practise aloud three times** and time yourself. Aim for around 2:30–2:45.
- **Look at Anika and Tomás**, not the whole room.
- **Pause after the bike story** — don’t rush the laugh.
- **Breathe before you start**, and hold your glass at the end so your hands have a job.

If you want, I can turn this into a full draft in your voice — just tell me your general tone: warm, funny, emotional, or all three.

long_N.input: Quick update, it's Friday October 3: last Sunday's long run was 12 km and the knee felt fine. Next week I'm in Lisbon for work Monday to Thursday and the hotel only has a treadmill. How should I adjust that week? Also, I'm vegetarian, in case that matters for fuelling.
long_N.reply:
Great news that the knee felt fine after 12 km. Without knowing your exact plan, I’d treat the Lisbon week as a maintenance/down week rather than trying to hit a full normal week on a treadmill.

Assuming your long run is usually Sunday:

- **Sun 5 Oct:** long run outdoors, repeat 12 km or add at most 1 km → **12–13 km**
- **Mon 6 Oct:** travel/rest, or easy 20 min treadmill if you feel stiff
- **Tue 7 Oct:** 30–40 min easy treadmill, 0.5–1% incline
- **Wed 8 Oct:** 30–40 min easy, or if knee feels good: 4–6 x 3 min moderate/tempo with 2 min easy
- **Thu 9 Oct:** 20–30 min easy treadmill or rest
- **Fri 10 Oct:** rest
- **Sun 12 Oct:** long run outdoors, **13–14 km** if everything still feels good

If your plan had a longer run scheduled during Mon–Thu, move it to Sunday before you leave or after you return, or cap it at **45–60 min easy on the treadmill**. Treadmill is fine for maintenance, but long treadmill runs are mentally and physically monotonous.

Treadmill tips: set incline around **0.5–1%**, go by effort rather than the treadmill’s speed display, hydrate well, and stop if the knee complains.

For vegetarian fuelling:

- Runs under ~75–90 min: no special fuelling needed, just normal meals and water.
- Long runs over ~75–90 min: practise taking **30–60 g carbs/hour**. Good travel-friendly options: bananas, dates, dried fruit, white bread with jam/honey, oat bars, pretzels, fruit juice, sports drink, vegetarian gels.
- Post-run: aim for **15–25 g protein + carbs** within 30–60 min. Eggs, Greek yogurt, cheese, tofu, lentils, beans, quinoa, or a pea/soy protein shake all work.
- Longer term as a vegetarian runner: keep an eye on **iron and B12**, and pair plant iron sources with vitamin C, e.g. lentils with peppers/orange.

long_N.reply:
Use pandas’ chunked reader. The main idea is to aggregate each chunk to **sums and counts**, then combine those aggregates at the end.

```python
import pandas as pd

path = "sensor_readings.csv"
chunksize = 300_000  # adjust based on your laptop

summaries = []

for chunk in pd.read_csv(
    path,
    chunksize=chunksize,
    parse_dates=["timestamp"],
):
    chunk["date"] = chunk["timestamp"].dt.date

    summary = (
        chunk.groupby(["date", "sensor_id"], as_index=False)
        .agg(
            temp_sum=("temperature", "sum"),
            humidity_sum=("humidity", "sum"),
            row_count=("timestamp", "count"),
        )
    )
    summaries.append(summary)

# Combine all chunk summaries
totals = (
    pd.concat(summaries)
    .groupby(["date", "sensor_id"], as_index=False)
    .agg(
        temp_sum=("temp_sum", "sum"),
        humidity_sum=("humidity_sum", "sum"),
        row_count=("row_count", "sum"),
    )
)

totals["avg_temperature"] = totals["temp_sum"] / totals["row_count"]
totals["avg_humidity"] = totals["humidity_sum"] / totals["row_count"]

result = totals[
    ["date", "sensor_id", "avg_temperature", "avg_humidity"]
].sort_values(["date", "sensor_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)

print(result)
```

This never loads the full 2 GB CSV into memory. It only keeps one chunk plus the much smaller per-chunk summaries.

If your timestamps are always ISO UTC as shown, you can avoid date parsing overhead by reading `timestamp` as a string and using:

```python
chunk["date"] = chunk["timestamp"].str[:10]
```

If you’re open to installing another library, Polars can do this more concisely with streaming:

```python
import polars as pl

df = (
    pl.scan_csv(path, try_parse_dates=True)
    .with_columns(pl.col("timestamp").dt.date().alias("date"))
    .group_by("date", "sensor_id")
    .agg(
        pl.col("temperature").mean().alias("avg_temperature"),
        pl.col("humidity").mean().alias("avg_humidity"),
    )
    .sort("date", "sensor_id")
    .collect(streaming=True)
)
```

long_N.input: My sourdough starter smells like nail polish remover and barely rises anymore. I feed it once a day with equal weights of flour and water and keep it on the kitchen counter, which is around 24 degrees. What is going wrong?
long_N.reply:
That nail-polish-remover/acetone smell is a classic sign that your starter is **hungry/over-fermented**—not necessarily ruined.

At 24°C, if you’re feeding once a day and carrying over a lot of starter, it can run out of food well before the next feed. The microbes then produce acidic/solvent-like byproducts, and the acid weakens the gluten, so the starter can’t trap gas and rise well.

**The fix is usually to feed a larger ratio of flour/water to starter, or feed more often.**

Try this reset for 2–3 days:

- Keep only **25 g starter**, discard the rest.
- Feed it **50 g flour + 50 g water** every **12 hours**.
- If you can only feed once a day, do **25 g starter + 100 g flour + 100 g water** once daily.
- Use unbleached flour and non-chlorinated water if possible.

Once it starts doubling reliably and smells mildly tangy/yeasty instead of like nail polish remover, it’s healthy again. After that, you can maintain it at 1:1:1 once or twice a day, or keep it in the fridge and feed weekly if you’re not baking daily.

long_N.input: Okay, I'll try twice-daily feeds. How long before I can bake with it again?
long_N.reply:
Assuming you switch to the **1:2:2 ratio** we mentioned — e.g. **25 g starter + 50 g flour + 50 g water** every 12 hours — it usually takes about **2–4 days** to recover, but go by signs rather than a fixed date.

It’s ready to bake when it:

- **Doubles or more within 4–6 hours** after feeding at 24°C  
- Smells **mildly tangy/yeasty**, not like nail polish remover  
- Looks **bubbly and billowy** throughout  

Optional test: drop a teaspoon of starter into water — if it **floats**, it has enough gas to leaven bread.

Once it’s doing that reliably, feed it and use it at its **peak rise** for baking. If it’s still sluggish after 5 days, try adding a little whole rye or whole wheat flour to the feed and make sure your water isn’t chlorinated.

long_N.reply:
```sql
WITH months AS (
    SELECT generate_series(
               '2026-01-01'::date,
               '2026-12-01'::date,
               interval '1 month'
           ) AS month_start
),
regions AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT region
    FROM customers
),
monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        c.region,
        date_trunc('month', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month_start,
        SUM(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'::timestamptz
      AND o.created_at <  '2027-01-01T00:00:00Z'::timestamptz
    GROUP BY
        c.region,
        date_trunc('month', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
)
SELECT
    m.month_start,
    r.region,
    COALESCE(mr.revenue, 0) AS revenue
FROM months m
CROSS JOIN regions r
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue mr
    ON mr.month_start = m.month_start
   AND mr.region = r.region
ORDER BY
    m.month_start,
    r.region;
```

This gives 12 months × every region, and uses `COALESCE` to show `0` for region/month combinations with no orders. The query groups and filters 2026 in UTC; if you want month boundaries in your session timezone instead, remove `AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'`.

long_N.input: Great. How would I add a column with the month-over-month percentage change?
long_N.reply:
You can wrap the monthly revenue results in a CTE/subquery, use `LAG()` to get the previous month’s revenue, and then calculate the percentage change.

```sql
WITH months AS (
    SELECT generate_series(
               '2026-01-01'::date,
               '2026-12-01'::date,
               interval '1 month'
           ) AS month_start
),
regions AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT region
    FROM customers
),
monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        c.region,
        date_trunc('month', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month_start,
        SUM(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'::timestamptz
      AND o.created_at <  '2027-01-01T00:00:00Z'::timestamptz
    GROUP BY
        c.region,
        date_trunc('month', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
),
month_region_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        m.month_start,
        r.region,
        COALESCE(mr.revenue, 0) AS revenue
    FROM months m
    CROSS JOIN regions r
    LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue mr
        ON mr.month_start = m.month_start
       AND mr.region = r.region
)
SELECT
    month_start,
    region,
    revenue,
    CASE
        WHEN prev_revenue IS NULL OR prev_revenue = 0 THEN NULL
        ELSE ROUND(((revenue - prev_revenue) / prev_revenue) * 100, 2)
    END AS mom_pct_change
FROM (
    SELECT
        month_start,
        region,
        revenue,
        LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue
    FROM month_region_revenue
) t
ORDER BY
    month_start,
    region;
```

Notes:

- The first month for each region will have `NULL` for `mom_pct_change` because there is no previous month.
- If the previous month’s revenue is `0`, the percentage change is mathematically undefined, so this query returns `NULL`. If you prefer `0` or another value in that case, change the `WHEN prev_revenue = 0 THEN NULL` branch.

long_N.input: My monstera has yellow leaves at the bottom and brown crispy edges on the newer ones. It's two metres from a north-facing window and I water it every Sunday. Any idea what's wrong?
long_N.reply:
Most likely: **overwatering combined with low light**.

A monstera 2 metres from a north-facing window gets fairly low light, so it uses water slowly. Watering every Sunday on a schedule often keeps the soil too wet. That can cause:

- **Yellow lower leaves** — classic overwatering/root stress sign.
- **Brown crispy edges on newer leaves** — the damaged roots can’t supply water properly, so the new growth dries at the edges. Low humidity can make this worse too.

### What I’d try

1. **Stop watering on a schedule.**  
   Check the soil first: water only when the top 3–5 cm feels dry. In that light, it might need water every 10–14 days, not weekly.

2. **Make sure the pot has drainage.**  
   It should never sit in water in a cover pot or saucer.

3. **Move it a bit closer to the window** if possible.  
   Monstera tolerates low light, but it does much better in bright indirect light.

4. **Check the roots** if the soil smells sour or stays wet.  
   If roots are mushy or dark, repot into a chunky, well-draining aroid mix after trimming rotten roots.

5. **For crisp edges**, once watering is fixed, you can raise humidity with a pebble tray or humidifier.

### Quick question
Does your pot have drainage holes, and is the soil still damp when you water on Sunday? That would confirm it’s an overwatering issue.

long_N.input: Should I repot it now or wait until spring?
long_N.reply:
It depends whether you suspect root rot or not.

**Repot now** if you see signs of root damage:
- Soil stays wet for many days after watering
- Sour or musty smell from the pot
- Yellowing is spreading quickly
- Stems feel soft near the soil

In that case, don’t wait — root rot only gets worse. Repot as soon as possible into a chunky, well-draining mix and trim any mushy roots.

**Wait** if the plant is otherwise stable and the soil dries out reasonably. Just adjust your watering first and let it recover. Repotting is stressful, so unnecessary repotting can make things worse.

One note: if you’re in the Northern Hemisphere, **it’s already spring now**, so this is actually a good time to repot anyway. If you’re in the Southern Hemisphere and it’s autumn, I’d only repot now if you suspect root rot; otherwise wait until spring.

Good news: since nothing has been pushed, you can rewrite local history safely.

But the important thing is: **removing the file in a new commit is not enough.** GitHub rejects the push because the 300 MB file is still reachable from earlier history. You need to purge it from the commits.

Your log looks like it has repeated/duplicated commit series, so I’d use `git filter-repo` rather than trying to rebase/drop only one commit.

## 1. Backup first

```bash
git branch backup/before-video-purge
```

## 2. Find the exact file path if needed

```bash
git ls-tree -r -l HEAD | sort -k 4 -n | tail -20
```

That should show the large video file near the bottom.

## 3. Install `git-filter-repo` if you don’t have it

```bash
python3 -m pip install git-filter-repo
```

Or on macOS:

```bash
brew install git-filter-repo
```

## 4. Purge the file from the feature branch history

Replace `path/to/video.mp4` with the actual path:

```bash
git filter-repo \
  --path path/to/video.mp4 \
  --invert-paths \
  --force \
  --refs "refs/heads/$(git branch --show-current)"
```

If there may be multiple video files:

```bash
git filter-repo \
  --path-glob '*.mp4' \
  --path-glob '*.mov' \
  --invert-paths \
  --force \
  --refs "refs/heads/$(git branch --show-current)"
```

## 5. Verify it’s gone from the branch

```bash
git log --oneline "$(git branch --show-current)" -- path/to/video.mp4
git rev-list --objects "$(git branch --show-current)" | grep path/to/video.mp4 || echo "clean"
```

The backup branch still contains the old history, so don’t verify with `--all`.

## 6. Push

Since you said nothing has been pushed yet:

```bash
git push -u origin "$(git branch --show-current)"
```

If the branch already exists on GitHub, use:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease origin "$(git branch --show-current)"
```

## Optional cleanup

After you’ve verified the push works, delete the backup branch:

```bash
git branch -D backup/before-video-purge
```

Then reclaim local disk space if you want:

```bash
git reflog expire --expire=now --all
git gc --prune=now --aggressive
```

Also make sure you don’t accidentally push the backup branch later.

long_N.input: Thanks. And how do I stop this happening again for video files?
long_N.reply:
Good question. The core rule:

> Never commit large binary files directly into Git history. Either ignore them or store them with Git LFS.

Here’s how to prevent this from happening again.

## 1. Add video files to `.gitignore` if you don’t need them versioned

Create or edit `.gitignore` in the repo root:

```gitignore
*.mp4
*.mov
*.avi
*.mkv
*.webm
*.wmv
*.flv
*.m4v
```

Then commit the `.gitignore` file itself:

```bash
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Ignore video files"
```

Now `git add .` or `git add --all` will not stage videos.  
Note: files already tracked before adding to `.gitignore` stay tracked, so if you accidentally commit one again, you’ll need to remove it from tracking with `git rm --cached path/to/video.mp4`.

## 2. If you DO need video files in the repo, use Git LFS

[Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com/) stores only a small pointer in Git and the actual file on LFS storage. GitHub allows LFS files, but there are storage/bandwidth quotas.

Install Git LFS:

```bash
git lfs install
```

Track video extensions:

```bash
git lfs track "*.mp4" "*.mov" "*.avi" "*.webm"
```

This creates/updates `.gitattributes`. Commit it:

```bash
git add .gitattributes
git commit -m "Track video files with Git LFS"
```

Now when you `git add` a video, Git will store it via LFS instead of as a regular object.

## 3. Add a pre-commit hook that blocks large files

Put this in `.git/hooks/pre-commit` and make it executable (`chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit`):

```bash
#!/bin/sh
# Reject files larger than 10 MB
max_bytes=$((10 * 1024 * 1024))

for file in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM); do
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then
        size=$(stat -c%s "$file")   # Linux
        # size=$(stat -f%z "$file") # macOS
        if [ "$size" -gt "$max_bytes" ]; then
            echo "ERROR: $file is larger than 10 MB ($size bytes)"
            echo "Use Git LFS or add it to .gitignore."
            exit 1
        fi
    fi
done
```

This runs automatically before every `git commit` and blocks oversized files.

If you use the `pre-commit` framework, you can add a hook like `check-added-large-files` with a size limit, but the shell script above is dependency-free.

## 4. Optional: Add a CI check for pull requests

In GitHub Actions you can add a step that runs:

```bash
! git diff --name-only HEAD^ | grep -E '\.(mp4|mov|avi|mkv|webm)$' || (echo "Video file found in commit" && exit 1)
```

But the pre-commit hook is usually enough.

---

**Summary:**  
- Don’t want videos in Git → add to `.gitignore`  
- Need videos in Git → use Git LFS  
- Add a size guard pre-commit hook as a safety net  

That should stop 300 MB video files from ever making it into history again.

long_N.input: A friend and I are planning a long weekend in the Lake District in spring, mostly for photography at sunrise and sunset. We'll have a car. Which areas and viewpoints would you suggest for three days?
long_N.reply:
Assuming you’re staying around **Keswick/Ambleside** and don’t want big hikes before dawn, a good three-day hit-list would be:

## Day 1 — Derwentwater, Borrowdale & Buttermere

**Sunrise:**  
- **Castlerigg Stone Circle** — easy, open sky, stone-foreground, often valley mist.  
- Alternative: **Latrigg** for a higher panoramic view over Keswick and Derwentwater.

**Morning:**  
- **Ashness Bridge** and **Surprise View** — classic Borrowdale viewpoints. Parking is small, so arrive early.  
- Optional short detour to **Watendlath Tarn**.

**Afternoon/evening:**  
- Drive over **Honister Pass** to **Buttermere**.  
- Photograph along the lakeshore path. The **Scots pines at the southern end** and the view towards **Fleetwith Pike / Haystacks** are classic.  
- The valley loses direct sun early, but blue hour and reflections can be excellent.

**Spring extra:** If you’re there late April–May, check **Rannerdale bluebells** near Crummock Water.

---

## Day 2 — Wastwater, Eskdale & Blea Tarn

**Early/sunrise:**  
- **Wastwater north shore pull-ins** — the classic view down the lake with the Screes and Scafell/Pillar behind.  
- Also stop at **Wasdale Head** for the Great Gable/Scafell backdrop.

**Midday:**  
- Either stay around Wasdale/Eskdale, or drive **Hardknott Pass** to Eskdale if you’re comfortable with steep hairpins.  
- Stop at **Boot / Eskdale Mill** if time allows.

**Sunset:**  
- If you return over **Wrynose Pass**, stop at **Blea Tarn** for reflections of the Langdale Pikes.  
- Otherwise head for **Tarn Hows** or **Coniston Water**.

---

## Day 3 — Langdale, Tarn Hows & Coniston

**Sunrise:**  
- **Blea Tarn** if you didn’t do it the previous evening — still water and Langdale Pikes reflections are superb.  
- Alternative: **Loughrigg Terrace** above Rydal Water/Grasmere.

**Morning:**  
- **Great Langdale valley** near **Elterwater** or around **Dungeon Ghyll** — barns, walls and the Langdale Pikes.

**Afternoon/sunset:**  
- **Tarn Hows** for easy reflections and fell views.  
- **Coniston Water** from around **Brantwood** or the southern end gives the Old Man of Coniston behind the lake.  
- **Kirkstone Pass** is a good moody alternative on the drive back.

---

If **Ullswater** fits your route better, swap a day for: sunrise at **Gowbarrow** or **Silver Bay**, **Aira Force**, and sunset around **Glenridding/Pooley Bridge**.

**Practical notes:**  
- Use PhotoPills or The Photographer’s Ephemeris to check sunrise/sunset direction.  
- A split base helps: e.g. 2 nights Keswick, 1 night Ambleside/Grasmere.  
- **Honister, Hardknott and Wrynose** are slow, narrow passes — allow extra time.  
- Bring a tripod, waterproofs and lens cloths. Spring weather changes fast, but that often gives the best light.

long_N.input: I need a regular expression that matches UK postcodes in free text, like SW1A 1AA or M1 1AE, but not random strings. Can you explain each part too?
long_N.reply:
Use this regex for free-text matching:

```regex
(?i)\b(?:[A-Z]{1,2}[0-9][A-Z0-9]?)\s?[0-9][A-Z]{2}\b
```

It matches common UK postcode shapes like `SW1A 1AA`, `M1 1AE`, `B33 8TH`.

### Explanation of each part

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `(?i)` | Case-insensitive matching, so `m1 1ae` also matches. |
| `\b` | Start at a word boundary, so it does not start in the middle of a longer word. |
| `(?:...)` | Non-capturing group for the outward postcode part. |
| `[A-Z]{1,2}` | One or two letters at the start, e.g. `SW`, `M`, `CR`. |
| `[0-9]` | The first district digit, e.g. `SW1A`, `M1`, `B33`. |
| `[A-Z0-9]?` | Optional extra district character: another digit for `B33`, or a letter for `SW1A`. |
| `\s?` | Optional single space between outward and inward parts. |
| `[0-9]` | Inward code digit, e.g. the `1` in `1AA`. |
| `[A-Z]{2}` | The final two letters, e.g. `AA`, `AE`. |
| `\b` | End at a word boundary. |

If you want to require the space, change `\s?` to `\s`.

Note: this checks the **shape** of a UK postcode, not whether it is actually allocated by Royal Mail. Made-up strings like `XX1 1XY` can still match because they have a valid shape.

long_N.input: I'm hosting a board game night for six adults who mostly haven't played modern games. We have about three hours. What games would work, and in what order?
long_N.reply:
For six adults new to modern games, I’d keep it social, easy to teach, and not over-schedule. With three hours, plan about four games plus a break.

A good order would be:

1. **Just One** — 3–7 players, ~20 min  
   Best opener. Cooperative, rule takes one minute, and people can drop in as they arrive.

2. **Sushi Go Party!** — 2–8 players, ~25 min  
   Light card-drafting. Cute, simple, gives everyone a first “real game” without heavy rules.

3. **Camel Up** — 2–8 players, ~35 min  
   Silly camel racing/betting game. Creates fun table moments.  
   Alternative: **King of Tokyo** — 2–6 players, ~30 min — if they’d prefer dice and monsters.

4. **Codenames** — 4–8+ players, ~30–40 min  
   Play 3 vs 3. Word-clue team game, very easy to teach, and you can play multiple rounds.

5. **Optional closer if time/energy allows:**  
   **The Resistance: Avalon** — 5–10 players, ~30 min — if the group enjoys bluffing/werewolf-style social deduction.  
   Or **Wavelength** — 2–12 players, ~20–30 min — for a lower-pressure discussion game.

**Why this order:** start cooperative/social, move into light strategy, then finish with team-based or social games once people are comfortable. Avoid heavier six-player games like **7 Wonders** or **Catan** as openers; they’re fine later, but teaching them can eat time and overwhelm first-timers.

If you want to keep purchases/borrowing minimal, the best three-game combo is probably **Just One, Camel Up, and Codenames**.

long_N.input: The rear derailleur on my commuter bike skips gears under load, especially on the middle cogs. I replaced the chain last month. What should I check first?
long_N.reply:
Check the **rear cogs/cassette first**, especially the middle ones.

A new chain on a worn cassette/freewheel is the classic cause of skipping under load. If the old chain was stretched, it wore the cogs to match; the new chain won’t sit fully into those worn teeth and will slip when you push hard.

Look for:

- “Shark fin” or hooked teeth on the middle cogs  
- A new chain that can be lifted slightly away from the cog at the 3 o’clock position  
- Visible grooves/ramps worn into the teeth

If the cassette/freewheel is worn, replace it—derailleur adjustment won’t fix that slip.

If the cogs look OK, then check in this order:

1. Derailleur hanger alignment  
2. Shift cable/housing friction or sticking  
3. Rear derailleur indexing/cable tension  
4. B-tension/chain gap

But given the new chain and the symptom, the cassette/freewheel is the likely culprit.

long_N.input: How do I adjust the cable tension with the barrel adjuster, step by step?
long_N.reply:
Here’s how to fine-tune rear derailleur cable tension with the barrel adjuster.

**First:** put the bike in a stand, flip it upside down, or ride on a quiet street so you can pedal while shifting.

### Step by step

1. **Shift to the smallest rear cog**  
   Use the shifter to move the chain onto the smallest cog.

2. **Click one gear up**  
   While pedaling, click the shifter once to shift to the second-smallest cog.

3. **Watch and listen to the shift**  
   - If the chain hesitates, rattles, or doesn’t move up cleanly:  
     **Turn the barrel adjuster counterclockwise** about **1/2 turn**  
     → this **adds cable tension**.
   - If the chain overshoots, tries to jump two cogs, or is noisy on the smaller cog:  
     **Turn the barrel adjuster clockwise** about **1/2 turn**  
     → this **reduces cable tension**.

4. **Repeat in small steps**  
   Make adjustments in **1/4 to 1/2 turn increments** until the shift from the smallest cog to the second cog is crisp.

5. **Shift through all the gears**  
   Run the shifter up and down the cassette.  
   - If the middle/larger cogs are slow to shift, add a little tension.  
   - If the smaller cogs are noisy or overshift, remove a little tension.

### Notes

- The barrel adjuster is usually where the cable housing enters the rear derailleur. On some bikes it’s at the shifter or inline on the cable.
- **Counterclockwise = more tension**, **clockwise = less tension** in most setups.
- If you run out of barrel adjuster range, you’ll need to re-clamp the cable at the derailleur pinch bolt.

This fixes indexing/rattling issues, but it won’t cure a worn cassette slipping under load. If the chain still skips after this, the cassette/freewheel remains the likely cause.

The cleanest fix is to let Postgres report when it’s actually ready via a healthcheck, then make `web` wait for that healthcheck.

`depends_on: [db]` only waits for the container to start, not for Postgres to accept connections.

Use Docker Compose’s long `depends_on` syntax with `condition: service_healthy`:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ['8000:8000']
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
    volumes: ['pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data']
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s

volumes:
  pgdata: {}
```

This makes Docker Compose start `db`, wait until `pg_isready` succeeds, and only then start `web`.

long_N.input: My dad is turning 65 and loves gardening, history podcasts and old maps. Budget about 80. Any gift ideas that aren't generic?
long_N.reply:
Since he likes gardening, history, and old maps, the sweet spot is probably the overlap: **historic garden plans, plant provenance maps, or local historical maps**.

A few non-generic ideas under $80:

1. **Framed old map of his town/county**  
   Go to the David Rumsey Map Collection online, find a high-res public-domain map of his hometown or region, download it, and have it printed at a local print shop. Add a simple frame. It’s personal, historical, and usually well under $80 if you skip custom framing.

2. **Historic garden plan print**  
   Search Etsy for “antique garden plan” or “vintage botanical map.” There are reproductions of 18th-century kitchen gardens, monastery gardens, and old botanical garden maps. That hits gardening + old maps + history at once.

3. **Heirloom seeds with a “provenance map”**  
   Buy a few heirloom varieties from somewhere like Seed Savers Exchange — especially ones with interesting histories, like Cherokee Purple tomatoes or Moon and Stars watermelon — and pair them with a small vintage-style world map. Mark where each variety originated. It feels curated, not generic.

4. **Custom vintage-style map centered on his garden/home**  
   Some Etsy sellers make personalized antique-style maps using his address or coordinates. Pair it with a small brass compass or a nice garden journal if the budget allows.

5. **Historic garden or historical society membership**  
   If there’s a local historic garden, arboretum, or historical society near him, a membership often costs $50–80 and includes talks, tours, plant sales, and sometimes member-only events. It’s a gift that keeps giving.

If you want, tell me his general region or a favorite history period — I can narrow it down more.

long_N.input: I'm learning Spanish on and off. I can order food and ask directions but freeze in real conversations. What routine would help in 20 minutes a day?
long_N.reply:
A 20-minute routine that helps with freezing should focus on **speaking out loud**, not just input. Try this daily:

**0–5 min: Listen & shadow**  
Pick a short dialogue or audio at your level. Play one sentence, pause, repeat it aloud with the same rhythm and intonation. Don’t worry about mistakes.

**5–10 min: Drill “survival chunks”**  
Practice phrases that buy you time in real conversations, until they feel automatic:
- ¿Me puedes repetir, por favor?
- No sé cómo se dice…
- ¿Qué significa…?
- Estoy aprendiendo español, ¿puedes hablar un poco más lento?
- Un momento, por favor.

**10–17 min: Speak alone, out loud**  
Choose a real scenario: ordering food, small talk, asking directions, talking about your weekend. Set a timer and speak for the full 7 minutes. Record yourself. If you get stuck, say the word in English and keep going.

**17–20 min: Review and fill the gap**  
Listen to your recording or note what you couldn’t say. Write down 1–2 new phrases to practice tomorrow.

The key is **daily production**, not perfection. If you can, add one short live conversation per week on an app like HelloTalk, Tandem, or iTalki so the solo practice transfers to real interaction.

For your level, start with **Chill Spanish Listening Practice**. The episodes are 5–10 minutes, spoken slowly and clearly, and cover everyday topics. That makes them ideal for the 5-minute shadowing part of your routine.

Once that feels easy, switch to **How to Spanish Podcast**. It’s more natural but still aimed at learners, and the YouTube version has subtitles if you need support.

long_N.input: 我想提前规划一下比赛前一周的饮食，你能帮我列一个大概的安排吗？
long_N.reply:
可以，我先按**耐力型比赛**（马拉松、长跑、自行车、足球赛等）给你一个通用模板。如果是力量/搏击/需要控体重的项目，饮食重点会不太一样，你可以告诉我项目再调整。

### 赛前一周饮食原则
- **逐步提高碳水比例**，给肌肉储存糖原。
- **蛋白质适量**，不要过量，避免增加消化负担。
- **脂肪偏低**，尤其赛前2—3天。
- **减少高纤维、产气食物**，如大量粗粮、豆类、韭菜、洋葱。
- **不碰没吃过的食物**，避免肠胃意外。
- **每天补水**，少量多次，观察尿色保持淡黄色。

---

### 7天大致安排

| 时间 | 重点 | 三餐思路 |
|---|---|---|
| **赛前7—5天** | 正常均衡，开始增加主食 | 早餐：燕麦/全麦面包+鸡蛋+水果；午餐：米饭/面条+瘦肉+蔬菜；晚餐：红薯/米饭+鱼/鸡胸+蔬菜。加餐：酸奶、香蕉、坚果少量。 |
| **赛前4—3天** | 高碳水、中蛋白、低油 | 主食占每餐一半以上，选白米饭、面条、馒头、土豆。蛋白质可以是鸡胸、鱼、蛋、豆腐。蔬菜选瓜类、胡萝卜、番茄等，减少粗纤维蔬菜。 |
| **赛前2天** | 继续高碳水，减少训练量 | 多选白米饭、白面包、白面条、馒头、土豆泥、香蕉、果汁。避免油炸、辛辣、豆类、大量生冷蔬菜。 |
| **赛前1天** | 易消化、少量多餐 | 早餐：白粥/馒头+香蕉；午餐：白米饭+鸡肉/鱼+少油瓜菜；晚餐：白面条或米饭+鱼+少量蔬菜。睡前可以加一小碗燕麦粥或半根香蕉。 |
| **比赛当天** | 熟悉、轻负担 | 赛前2.5—4小时吃：白面包/馒头/米饭+少量花生酱或鸡蛋+香蕉。赛前1小时可喝运动饮料或吃半根香蕉。避免高脂肪、高纤维、大量蛋白质。 |

---

### 补水建议
- 赛前一周每天喝 **2—3升水**，不要等渴了再喝。
- 赛前2—3天可以适量喝含电解质的饮料，但不要过量。
- 比赛前1天避免大量咖啡、酒精，咖啡因如果平时没试过就不要临时喝。

---

### 特别提醒
如果你比赛超过 **90分钟**，这种“高碳水填充”会有帮助。如果是短时间爆发力项目，正常均衡饮食就够，不必极端碳水填充。

你可以告诉我比赛项目和具体时间，我可以帮你把比赛当天早餐时间也细化一下。

long_N.reply:
比赛前一晚的关键是：**高碳水、适量蛋白质、低脂肪、低纤维、好消化、不尝新**。目的是把糖原补足，同时不让肠胃有负担，保证睡眠。

### 推荐晚餐时间
最好安排在 **18:00—19:30** 之间吃完，不要拖到太晚。如果第二天比赛很早，可以提前到 17:30—18:30。

---

### 晚餐可以这样搭配

**方案一：稳妥米饭型**
- 白米饭/白粥/软米饭 1—1.5碗
- 清蒸鱼或鸡胸肉/去皮的鸡腿肉 一小份
- 少量易消化蔬菜：冬瓜、西葫芦、胡萝卜、番茄、土豆
- 少油少盐，不要红烧、油炸

**方案二：面食型**
- 清汤面条/番茄鸡蛋面/鸡汤面
- 面条量可以多一些
- 配一个鸡蛋或少量瘦肉
- 蔬菜选切成小块煮软的，比如番茄、小白菜叶、菠菜叶

**方案三：粥+馒头型**
- 白粥或小米粥
- 白馒头/花卷 1—2个
- 清蒸鱼/鸡蛋羹
- 少量土豆丝或胡萝卜丝

---

### 赛前一晚尽量避免
- 大量粗粮、全麦、豆类、韭菜、洋葱、西兰花、生冷沙拉：容易胀气
- 油炸、肥肉、火锅、烧烤、麻辣：消化负担重
- 大量奶制品：如果平时喝了没事可以，但不要临时喝很多
- 酒精、咖啡因：影响睡眠和恢复
- 没吃过的新食物、补剂、奇怪的“能量餐”

---

- 半根香蕉
- 一小碗白粥/燕麦粥
- 2—3 片苏打饼干
- 几口白面包

不要吃撑，垫一下就行。

---

long_N.input: I bought a hand grinder and a V60. My coffee tastes sour and thin. I'm using 15 g coffee to 250 g water just off the boil. What should I change first?
long_N.reply:
Change one thing first: **grind finer**.

Sour + thin is usually under-extraction. Your ratio (15 g / 250 g) and water temp are fine, so the most likely issue is the grind is too coarse.

- Go **finer in small steps**—about 2–4 clicks or one notch, depending on the grinder.
- Keep everything else the same.
- If it’s still sour, go finer again.
- If it suddenly tastes bitter, dry, or harsh, back off slightly coarser.

A rough sanity check: for 15 g / 250 g on a V60, total brew time is often around **2:00–2:45**. If yours is draining much faster than that, the grind is almost certainly too coarse.

What hand grinder are you using? That would help me give a more specific starting range.
long_N.host_user_content: I bought a hand grinder and a V60. My coffee tastes sour and thin. I'm using 15 g coffee to 250 g water just off the boil. What should I change first?

long_N.input: How fine is 'finer' in practice?
long_N.reply:
A practical target is **medium-fine** — roughly like **fine table salt or caster sugar**, not like flour or espresso powder.

Practical checks:

- **Look/feel:** If your current grounds look like coarse sea salt or rough sand with clearly visible chunks, they’re too coarse. You want them to feel gritty but not powdery. When you pinch them, they may clump just a little.
- **Brew time:** For 15 g / 250 g in a V60, aim for roughly **2:15–2:45 total drawdown**. If it’s draining well under 2:00, it’s usually a sign to go finer.
- **Adjustment size:**  
  - Stepped grinder: try **2–4 clicks finer** at a time.  
  - Stepless grinder: make a small but noticeable movement, maybe around **1/8 turn finer**.

Then brew again and adjust by taste. If it starts tasting bitter, dry, or harsh, you went a bit too fine — back off 1–2 clicks.

long_N.input: Ugh. Today is Wednesday, November 5. I ran yesterday and again this morning to make up for a missed session, and now my knee is sore. What should I do for the rest of this week?
long_N.reply:
That sounds like an overuse reaction from running back-to-back to “catch up.” For the rest of this week, I’d treat the knee as the priority, not the missed mileage.

**Do this:**
- **Rest today and Thursday from running.** Let the soreness settle.
- **Ice** for 10–15 minutes at a time if there’s swelling or warmth, especially after activity.
- **Walk normally if it’s pain-free.** If walking hurts or you’re limping, back off more.
- **Avoid deep squats, lunges, hills, or hard surfaces** until it feels normal.

**Later this week:**
- If by **Friday or Saturday** the knee feels fine walking, you could try a short, easy run—but stop if pain comes back.
- If it’s still sore, skip running this weekend and consider low-impact cross-training like swimming or easy cycling **only if it doesn’t hurt the knee**.

**Important:** Don’t double up sessions to make up for missed ones—it usually causes exactly this. It’s better to skip a missed run than lose a week to knee pain.

See a physio or sports med professional if you have swelling, sharp pain, locking/giving way, or if it’s not improving after several days.

long_N.input: My car insurance renewal went up 40 percent with no claims. What questions should I ask before switching, and what usually lowers the price?
long_N.reply:
That is frustrating, and unfortunately a 40% jump with no claims can still happen due to inflation, repair costs, weather losses, or statewide rate increases. Here are the key questions to ask and ways to lower your price.

## Questions to ask your current insurer before switching

1. **Why exactly did my rate go up?**  
   Ask if it’s a personal change or a general rate increase.

2. **Is my policy information accurate?**  
   Check annual mileage, garaging address, drivers, and vehicle use. Overestimated mileage can raise your rate.

3. **Can you re-quote or review my discounts?**  
   Ask about multi-policy, paperless billing, autopay, alumni/employer/professional discounts, defensive driving, and telematics.

4. **What would my price be with a higher deductible?**  
   This can show you potential savings without switching.

5. **Am I paying for coverage I don’t need?**  
   Ask about rental reimbursement, towing/roadside assistance, or collision/comprehensive on an older vehicle.

6. **Are there any retention or loyalty discounts available?**  
   Sometimes insurers have unadvertised retention offers.

7. **If I switch mid-term, are there cancellation fees?**  
   Know what it costs to leave.

## Before switching to another insurer

1. **Is this quote for the same coverage?**  
   Compare identical liability limits, deductibles, and optional coverages.

2. **Is the quote binding?**  
   Ask if the price can change after underwriting reviews your driving history, credit, or claims.

3. **Are all fees included?**  
   Some quotes omit installment fees or policy fees.

4. **Does the quote include a new-customer discount?**  
   Ask if the price will jump next year when that discount falls off.

5. **What is the insurer’s reputation?**  
   Check financial strength and complaint records, not just price.

6. **Do they offer accident forgiveness or claim-free benefits?**  
   This can protect you later.

7. **Do they offer telematics or usage-based discounts?**  
   Ask what data is collected and how it affects your rate.

## What usually lowers car insurance prices

- **Raise your deductible** — moving from $500 to $1,000 can lower premiums meaningfully, but make sure you can afford the deductible if you have a claim.
- **Drop collision/comprehensive on older cars** — if your car is worth only a few thousand dollars, you may be paying more than the coverage is worth.
- **Bundle policies** — auto + renters/home/umbrella with the same insurer often brings a big discount.
- **Lower or correct your annual mileage** — if you drive less than estimated, report it.
- **Try a telematics/safe-driving program** — careful drivers often save.
- **Take a defensive driving course** — some insurers offer discounts for approved courses.
- **Pay annually instead of monthly** — installment fees add up.
- **Improve your credit-based insurance score** — where allowed, better credit can lower rates.
- **Shop around every year or two** — independent agents and direct insurers can compare rates.
- **Check group or affinity discounts** — employers, alumni associations, professional groups, and credit unions sometimes have deals.
- **Don’t cancel your old policy until the new one is active** — a coverage lapse can make you more expensive to insure.

If you get a lower quote elsewhere, you can also give your current insurer a chance to match or beat it before switching.

long_N.input: Is it worth adding a named driver?
long_N.reply:
It depends on **who** the named driver is and whether they actually use the car. It’s not a guaranteed discount, and sometimes it can backfire.

## When adding a named driver may help

- A **spouse or partner with a clean record, good credit/insurance score, and several years’ driving experience** may lower your premium slightly. Insurers often view married or partnered households as lower risk.
- If the named driver is **lower risk than you** and will be the **primary driver**, that can reduce the premium compared to you being listed as primary.
- Adding a driver can sometimes unlock a **multi-driver or household discount**, but this varies by insurer.

## When it will probably hurt

- Adding a **teen, newly licensed, or high-risk driver** will almost always raise your premium.
- Adding anyone with **accidents, tickets, or poor credit-based insurance score** can increase the rate.
- Even adding a low-risk driver may raise the price slightly because it adds another person with potential access to the car.

## Important rules to avoid problems

- If the person **lives in your household and drives your car regularly**, you usually **must list them** on the policy. Not listing them can be considered misrepresentation and could lead to a claim being denied.
- If the person **does not live with you and rarely drives your car**, you generally don’t need to add them.
- If someone in your household is high risk but will **never drive your car**, ask about a **driver exclusion**. This can lower your premium, but that person would have **no coverage** if they did drive.

## Best way to know

Ask your insurer or agent:

> “Can you quote my policy **with and without** adding [person] as a named driver?”

Also ask:

- Does it matter if they are listed as **primary vs occasional**?
- Is there a **multi-driver or household discount**?
- Would adding them change my **coverage or claims eligibility**?

Don’t add someone just to manipulate the rate if they don’t actually drive the car—that can cause coverage problems later.

long_N.input: My nephew turns seven next month and I offered to plan games for ten kids in a small garden for two hours. Ideas that don't need much equipment?
long_N.reply:
A small garden is totally doable. For seven-year-olds, keep each game short—about 10–15 minutes max—and have water/shade ready.

### Low/no-equipment games

- **What’s the Time, Mr Wolf?**  
  One child is the wolf. Kids call out the question, wolf says times, then shouts “Dinner time!” and chases them. Set clear garden boundaries.

- **Red Light, Green Light**  
  One child is the traffic light. Green = move, red = freeze. Anyone caught moving goes back.

- **Simon Says**  
  Classic and great for garden groups. No equipment.

- **Musical Statues / Freeze Dance**  
  Use a phone speaker. Dance when music plays, freeze when it stops.

- **Duck, Duck, Goose**  
  Sit in a circle, one child taps heads and runs. Good with 10 kids.

- **Sleeping Lions**  
  All kids lie still like lions. One or two “hunters” try to make them laugh/move without touching them. Great for calming down.

- **Hot Potato**  
  Use a scrunched-up sock or small ball. Pass while music plays; whoever holds it when music stops does a silly task or sits out briefly.

- **Charades / Animal Charades**  
  Act out animals, jobs, or actions. No equipment needed.

- **Telephone / Chinese Whispers**  
  Whisper a phrase around the circle and see how it changes.

- **Wink Murder**  
  One secret winker “kills” players by winking, a detective guesses who it is. Very low-energy.

- **Human Knot**  
  Split into two groups of five. Everyone grabs hands randomly and tries to untangle without letting go.

- **Garden Scavenger Hunt**  
  Call out things to find: something green, tiny, rough, round, etc. No collecting needed if you want zero mess.

### Optional cheap extras
If you’re happy with a tiny bit of equipment:
- **Balloons** – keepy-uppy or balloon between knees relay.
- **Chalk** – draw hopscotch, targets, or a start/finish line.
- **Pass the Parcel** – wrapped parcel, music from phone.

### Sample 2-hour flow
- **0:00–0:10** – Arrival: name game or simple animal charades  
- **0:10–0:30** – What’s the Time, Mr Wolf? + Red Light, Green Light  
- **0:30–0:50** – Musical Statues / Freeze Dance  
- **0:50–1:10** – Duck, Duck, Goose + Hot Potato  
- **1:10–1:25** – Snack/drink break  
- **1:25–1:40** – Garden Scavenger Hunt  
- **1:40–1:50** – Sleeping Lions or Telephone  
- **1:50–2:00** – Wind down, cake, happy birthday

The key is alternating active games with calmer ones, especially in a small space.

long_N.reply:
Your biggest `/var` consumers are:

- `/var/log` — 6.0G
- `/var/lib` — 11G

Those need deeper drill-down. Also check the whole root filesystem, because the 95% full disk may include `/home`, `/usr`, `/snap`, `/root`, etc.

## 1. Get the full root-disk picture

```bash
sudo du -h -x --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -30
```

`-x` keeps it on the same filesystem.

## 2. Drill into the large directories

```bash
sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var/log | sort -h | tail -20
sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var/lib | sort -h | tail -20
```

If `/var/lib/docker` exists and is large:

```bash
sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var/lib/docker 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -20
docker system df
```

## 3. Safe cleanups to start with

### Journal / systemd logs

```bash
journalctl --disk-usage
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M
sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=7d
```

### Apt cache and old kernels

```bash
sudo apt clean
sudo apt autoremove --purge
```

### Find the largest files in `/var/log`

```bash
sudo find /var/log -type f -printf '%s %p\n' | sort -nr | head -20
```

You can often safely remove or compress old rotated logs like `*.gz` or `*.old`, but don’t delete active `.log` files blindly.

## 4. Be careful with `/var/lib`

`/var/lib` usually contains state/data for services:

- `mysql`
- `postgresql`
- `docker`
- `snapd`
- `dpkg`
- `apt`

Do **not** delete files there unless you know exactly what they are.

If snap packages are taking space:

```bash
sudo du -h /var/lib/snapd/snaps 2>/dev/null | sort -h
```

Old snap revisions can be removed with:

```bash
sudo snap set system refresh.retain=2
```

## Next step

Paste the output of this if you want help interpreting it:

```bash
sudo du -h -x --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -30
```

That will show whether `/var` is actually the main problem, or whether something else on the root disk is also large.

long_N.input: Journal logs are 6 GB. How do I cap them permanently?
long_N.reply:
To cap journal logs permanently, set a size limit in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`.

## 1. Edit the journald configuration

```bash
sudo nano /etc/systemd/journald.conf
```

Find or add these lines under the `[Journal]` section:

```ini
[Journal]
SystemMaxUse=500M
SystemKeepFree=2G
SystemMaxFileSize=100M
```

What they do:

- `SystemMaxUse=500M` — max total size of persistent journal logs
- `SystemKeepFree=2G` — ensure at least 2 GB stays free on the filesystem
- `SystemMaxFileSize=100M` — max size of each journal file

Adjust the values to your preference. For example, if you want a 1 GB cap:

```ini
SystemMaxUse=1G
```

## 2. Restart the journal service

```bash
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
```

## 3. Immediately shrink the existing 6 GB of logs

The config applies going forward, but you should also vacuum the current logs now:

```bash
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M
```

Or if you already set the cap to 1 GB:

```bash
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=1G
```

## 4. Verify

```bash
journalctl --disk-usage
```

You should see the journal reduced to around the limit you set.

---

If you want an even stricter approach, you can also set `Storage=volatile` to keep logs only in RAM instead of disk, but that means logs disappear on reboot. I’d recommend keeping persistent storage with the size cap above.

**1. Open with intent, not apology**

**2. Lead with impact in 3–4 points**

I automated the monthly vendor report, saving about six hours a month. I also ran the data quality working group, presented Q2 results to leadership, and mentored two junior analysts through their first quarter.”

**3. Connect it to expanded scope**  
Make the case that you’re already operating above your current level.

> “These responsibilities go beyond what I was originally hired to do, and I’ve been taking on more leadership and ownership across the team.”

**4. Make a specific ask**  
Don’t leave it vague. Have a number or range ready.

> “Based on that expanded scope and market data for similar roles, I’m asking for a base salary adjustment to [$X] / of [X%].”

Then stop and let them respond.

**5. Handle the response**

- If yes:  
  > “Thank you. What timeline should I expect for that to take effect?”

- If maybe/not now:  
  > “What specific outcomes would make this possible by next quarter?”

- If no:  
  > “I understand. Can we agree on a review date and a target to work toward?”

- Research market pay for your role/title and location.  
- Decide your target number and a minimum you’d accept.  
- Bring a one-page summary of your accomplishments with the numbers.  
- Avoid framing the raise around personal need, cost of living, or what coworkers make. Keep it about the value you’ve created.

long_N.input: What if my manager says the budget is frozen?
long_N.reply:
“Budget is frozen” is a common first response, but it doesn’t have to end the conversation. The key is to stay calm, ask good questions, and pivot to what *is* possible.

### 1. Clarify what “frozen” actually means

Don’t just accept it and back off. Ask:

> “I understand budgets can be tight. Can you help me understand — is this a company-wide freeze, or specific to our team? And is it temporary?”

This does two things: it shows you’re not being difficult, and it tells you whether there’s any flexibility.

You can also ask:

> “Is there a timeline for when the budget is expected to reopen, or a typical review cycle when adjustments are considered?”

### 2. Ask about exceptions or alternatives

If base salary is truly frozen, there may be other levers:

- One-time bonus or retention bonus  
- Title change to reflect your current scope  
- Extra PTO or flexible work arrangement  
- Professional development budget  
- Equity, if relevant  
- A written commitment to revisit salary at a specific date  

You could say:

> “If base salary can’t move right now, I’d like to talk about what’s possible. For example, is there room for a title change to match the scope I’ve taken on, or a one-time bonus? And can we agree on a date to revisit the salary conversation?”

### 3. Lock in a clear follow-up plan

If they can’t give you a raise now, make it concrete. Avoid leaving it open-ended.

> “I appreciate that. Can we set a specific review date — say, in 90 days — and agree on the milestones that would justify the adjustment at that point? I’d like to make sure this isn’t lost.”

Then after the meeting, send a short email summarizing:

> “Thanks for the conversation today. As discussed, budget is currently frozen, but we agreed to revisit my compensation on [date], contingent on [specific milestones]. I’ll continue focusing on those outcomes.”

That creates a paper trail and keeps them accountable.

### 4. What to avoid

- Don’t say “okay, never mind” and drop it completely.  
- Don’t threaten to quit unless you’re actually prepared to leave.  
- Don’t compare yourself to coworkers or say “but X got a raise.”  
- Don’t frame it as personal need — keep it about the value you’ve created.

### 5. If it’s truly a dead end

If there’s no raise, no alternative, no timeline, and no plan, that’s useful information too. It tells you something about how the company values your growth.

You can end the conversation professionally:

> “I understand. If there’s no path forward on compensation right now, can we check in again at the start of next quarter? In the meantime, I’ll keep documenting the impact of the work I’m doing.”

Then, quietly, you can decide whether to start exploring external options. Having that conversation often gives you clarity either way.

- Label four boxes/bags: **Donate**, **Bin**, **Elsewhere**, **Decide later**.
- Clear one table or floor area for paperwork.

## Saturday plan

### 9:00–9:15 — Start properly
- Eat something, get dressed, put shoes on.
- Write down **3 goals for the day**, not 10:
  1. Clear the main living floor.
  2. Fix or make a decision about the broken shelf.
  3. Get all paperwork into one sorted place.

### 9:15–10:30 — Unpack main living area
- Work **one box at a time**.
- Rule: every item either gets a home now, or goes into Donate / Bin / Elsewhere.
- Have a basket for “belongs in another room” and only deliver it after the timer ends.

### 10:30–10:45 — Break
Open windows, water, quick reset.

### 10:45–11:45 — Continue unpacking
Focus on whichever room will make Monday easiest: usually **bedroom** or **kitchen**.

### 11:45–12:30 — Paperwork round 1
- Gather all loose paperwork into one pile.
- Sort fast into three piles only:
  - **Action** — bills, forms, things with deadlines
  - **File** — keep but no action
  - **Shred/recycle**
- Don’t read everything in detail. If it takes more than 30 seconds to decide, put it in Action and move on.

### 12:30–13:15 — Lunch
Leave the flat or sit away from the mess. Don’t multitask.

### 13:15–14:00 — Broken shelf
- Diagnose the problem.
- If it’s fixable in about **20–30 minutes**, fix it.
- If not, make a decision: order missing parts now, bin it, or move it to a “fix later” corner.
- Don’t let the shelf eat the whole day.

### 14:00–15:30 — Unpacking focus: kitchen/bathroom
These rooms give quick visible wins and make the flat feel functional again.

### 15:30–15:45 — Break

### 15:45–16:45 — Paperwork round 2
- Take the **Action pile** and put it into one folder or box.
- Add a 30-minute reminder for Monday to actually process it.
- Recycle/shred the obvious junk now.
- Put the **File pile** somewhere out of sight.

### 16:45–17:15 — Reset
- Flatten empty boxes.
- Take rubbish/recycling out.
- Wipe main surfaces or hoover the main walkway.
- Put tools away.

### 17:15 onwards — Done
Shower, order food, or go for a walk. Don’t start new tasks.

By Saturday evening, aim for:
- Main floor clear and flat livable.
- Essentials reachable for Monday morning.
- Paperwork in one place, with a plan to handle action items.
- Broken shelf fixed, binned, or clearly parked for later.
